questions.title: DNS
questions.text: State what DNS stands for and describe its purpose.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Domain Name System (1)
- translates / resolves domain names into IP addresses (1)
scheme.model_answer: Domain Name System — it converts domain names such as nis.edu.kz into the IP addresses computers use.

questions.title: Name and IP
questions.text: Describe the relationship between an IP address and a domain name, and explain why domain names are used.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The IP address is the numerical identifier of the server the domain name represents (1)
- domain names are easier for people to remember / type than numbers (1)
scheme.model_answer: A domain name is a text label for the server's IP address; people use names because they are much easier to remember than numbers.

questions.title: Domain levels
questions.text: Complete the table for the domain name **www.ast.nis.edu.kz**.

scheme.mark_scheme: kz (1); edu (1); nis (1); www (1)

questions.title: Second-level domain
questions.text: State the second-level domain name of the website **www.portal.gov.kz**.

scheme.mark_scheme: gov (1)

questions.title: Types of TLD
questions.text: Tick (✓) whether each top-level domain is generic or a country code.

scheme.mark_scheme: country; generic; country; generic (1 each)

questions.title: DNS servers
questions.text: Match each DNS server to its role.

right.text: Searches on behalf of the user's computer, usually run by the ISP
Refers requests to the server for the correct top-level domain
Knows which servers hold each domain ending in, e.g., .kz
Stores the actual IP address records for one domain

questions.title: Order of a lookup
questions.text:
The steps of a DNS lookup are in the wrong order:

- **A** The resolver asks the root server
- **B** The browser checks its cache
- **C** The browser connects to the web server using the IP address
- **D** The authoritative server returns the IP address

Write the letters in the correct order.

scheme.mark_scheme: B, A, D, C (1 each)

questions.title: Caching
questions.text: Explain why DNS answers are cached by browsers and resolvers.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The IP address can be found without asking other DNS servers again (1)
- faster page loading / less DNS traffic / less load on servers (1)
scheme.model_answer: The stored IP address can be used next time without repeating the whole lookup, so websites open faster and there is less traffic to DNS servers.

questions.title: Distributed system
questions.text: Explain why DNS is distributed across many servers rather than stored on one central server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): too many names / requests for one server; no single point of failure / more reliable; faster — servers close to users; each organisation manages its own records
scheme.model_answer: One server could not hold billions of names or answer every request, and if it failed the whole Internet would stop working by name; many servers share the load and keep it reliable.

questions.title: DNS records
questions.text: Match each DNS record type to what it stores.

right.text: The IPv4 address of a name
The mail server for the domain
An alias pointing to another name

scheme.mark_scheme: A–IPv4, MX–mail, CNAME–alias.

questions.title: DNS spoofing
questions.text: Explain how DNS cache poisoning can be used to steal users' passwords.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- An attacker puts a false IP address for a real domain into a DNS cache (1)
- users typing the correct name are sent to a fake website that collects their login details (pharming) (1)
scheme.model_answer: The attacker changes the cached IP address for, say, a bank's domain to the address of a fake copy of the site; users type the right name but land on the fake page and enter their passwords.

questions.title: Parts of a URL
questions.text: For the URL **https://www.shop.kz/catalog/phones.html?brand=x#top**, complete the table.

scheme.mark_scheme: https; www.shop.kz; /catalog/; phones.html; brand=x (1 each)

questions.title: URL
questions.text: Describe the role of a URL.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Uniform Resource Locator — the full address of a resource on the web (1)
- tells the browser the protocol, the server (domain) and the location / file of the resource (1)
scheme.model_answer: A URL is the unique address of a web resource; it tells the browser which protocol to use, which server to contact and where the file is on that server.

questions.title: Write a URL
questions.text: Give one example of a URL that shows a **protocol**, a **host name** and a **file location**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any valid URL with all three parts, e.g. http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/George.jpg (1)

questions.title: Port number
questions.text: Which port is used by default for **HTTPS**?

scheme.mark_scheme: D

questions.title: URL or domain
questions.text: A domain name is one part of a URL.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: Accessing a website
questions.text: A domain name is an easy-to-remember representation of an IP address.

parts.title: Explain
parts.text: Explain how the domain name is used to access a website. Include the role of Domain Name System (DNS) servers in your explanation.

scheme.mark_scheme: Up to 5 (1 each): user types URL / domain into browser; browser checks its cache / hosts file; request sent to DNS server / resolver which holds a list of domain names and IP addresses; if not found, request passed to other DNS servers (root → TLD → authoritative); IP address returned to the browser and cached; browser uses the IP address to contact the web server and request the page; error if name not found
scheme.model_answer: The user types the domain name in the browser, which first checks its cache. If the IP address is not there, it asks the DNS resolver, which looks it up and, if needed, asks a root server, then the .kz TLD server, then the domain's authoritative server. The IP address is returned and cached, and the browser uses it to connect to the web server and request the page.

parts.title: Second level
parts.text: State the second-level domain name of the website **www.sk.nis.edu.kz**.

scheme.mark_scheme: edu (1)

parts.title: Relationship
parts.text: Describe the relationship between the IP address and the domain name.

scheme.mark_scheme: The IP address is the numerical identifier for the domain name, used to reach the website (1)
scheme.model_answer: The domain name stands for the server's IP address, which is the number actually used to reach the website.

parts.title: Caching
parts.text: Explain **one** benefit of caching DNS results.

scheme.mark_scheme: No need to repeat the full lookup (1); faster access / less network traffic / less load on DNS servers (1)
scheme.model_answer: The IP address is already stored, so the lookup does not have to be repeated and the site opens faster.

questions.title: Domain hierarchy
questions.text: The website of a school has the address **https://www.ast.nis.edu.kz/news/2026/sports.html**.

scheme.mark_scheme: https; www.ast.nis.edu.kz; /news/2026/; sports.html (1 each)

parts.title: TLD
parts.text: Identify the top-level domain and state its type.

scheme.mark_scheme: kz — country code TLD (1)

parts.title: Protocol
parts.text: Explain why the URL begins with https rather than http.

scheme.mark_scheme: HTTPS is the secure version of HTTP (1); data between browser and server is encrypted so it cannot be read / changed if intercepted (1)
scheme.model_answer: HTTPS encrypts the data sent between the browser and the school's server, so it cannot be read or altered if intercepted.

questions.title: DNS servers
questions.text: DNS is a distributed, hierarchical system of servers.

parts.title: Server roles
parts.text: Describe the role of each server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Root: refers to the correct TLD server (1). TLD: knows the servers responsible for domains in that TLD (1). Authoritative: holds the records / IP address for the domain and returns it (1)
scheme.model_answer: Root: points the resolver to the server for the top-level domain. TLD server: points to the servers holding a particular domain. Authoritative server: stores the domain's IP address and gives it to the resolver.

parts.title: Distributed
parts.text: Explain **two** advantages of DNS being distributed across many servers.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): shares the load of billions of requests; no single point of failure; faster responses from nearby servers; each organisation updates its own records
scheme.model_answer: The huge number of requests is shared between many servers, and if one server fails others still answer.

parts.title: Risk
parts.text: Explain how an attacker could misuse DNS to direct users to a fake website, and **one** way to protect against this.

scheme.mark_scheme: False IP address inserted into DNS cache / server (1); users typing the real name reach the fake site and may enter personal data (1); protection: DNSSEC / check HTTPS certificate / trusted DNS resolver (1)
scheme.model_answer: By DNS cache poisoning, the attacker stores a fake IP address for a real domain, so users are sent to a copy of the site and give away passwords. DNSSEC signs DNS records so false ones can be detected.

summary: Why the Domain Name System is needed, the relationship between domain names and IP addresses, the hierarchy of domain names and DNS servers, how a domain name is resolved step by step (with caching), common DNS records and risks, and the structure of a URL.

blocks.content: Every device on the Internet is identified by an **IP address** such as `185.22.66.10`. Computers use these numbers to send data, but people find them **hard to remember**. Instead we type **domain names** such as `nis.edu.kz`.
An **easy-to-remember text name** that represents the **IP address** of a server (or group of servers), e.g. `nis.edu.kz`, `google.com`.

A **distributed, hierarchical** system of **servers** that **translates domain names into IP addresses** (this is called **name resolution**), so that people can use names while computers use numbers.

items.title: Relationship between IP address and domain name
items.content:
- The IP address is the **numerical identifier** behind the domain name.
- One domain name can point to **several** IP addresses (large sites use many servers), and one server IP can host **many** domain names.
- If a website moves to a new server, only the **DNS record** changes — users keep typing the same name.

items.title: Why DNS is distributed
items.content:
- No single server could store **billions** of names or answer every request.
- Data is spread across **millions** of servers worldwide, so the system is **fast** and has **no single point of failure**.
- Each organisation manages the records for **its own** domain.

blocks.title: IP address vs domain name
blocks.content:
| Domain name | Example IP address |
|---|---|
| `nis.edu.kz` | 185.22.66.10 (example) |
| `google.com` | 142.250.74.46 |
| `localhost` | 127.0.0.1 (your own computer) |
Domain names are **hierarchical** and are read **from right to left**, from the most **general** level to the most **specific**, separated by dots.

rows: A particular school of the network

          │                  ┌────┴────┐

                             │

                        │

blocks.caption: The domain name hierarchy (a tree)

blocks.title: Who manages names?
blocks.content: **ICANN** coordinates the root and the TLDs worldwide. Names in `.kz` are registered through accredited **registrars**; the owner pays to register a name for a period (usually a year) and chooses which **DNS servers** hold its records.
"State the **second-level** domain of www.sk.nis.edu.kz" → **edu**. Count from the **right**: kz = top (1st) level, edu = 2nd, nis = 3rd.

theory.title: How a domain name is resolved

items.title: Types of DNS server
items.content:
- **Resolver (recursive DNS server)** — usually run by the **ISP** or the school; does the searching for the user's computer.
- **Root servers** — know the servers of every **TLD**.
- **TLD servers** — e.g. the `.kz` server knows which servers hold each `.kz` domain.
- **Authoritative server** — stores the actual **records** for one domain, e.g. `nis.edu.kz`.

items.title: Caching
items.content:
- Answers are **stored (cached)** for a time (the **TTL**, time to live) by the browser, the operating system and the resolver.
- Repeat visits are **much faster** and DNS traffic is reduced.

blocks.content:
Browser ──1──► Resolver (ISP)          1  "What is the IP of www.nis.edu.kz?"
                   │  ▲
                   2  3                  2/3 Root server: "ask the .kz TLD server"
                   │  │
                   ├──┴──► Root server
                   4  5                  4/5 .kz server: "ask the nis.edu.kz server"
                   ├──┴──► .kz TLD server
                   6  7                  6/7 Authoritative server: "185.22.66.10"
                   └──┴──► nis.edu.kz authoritative server
  Browser ◄──8── Resolver                8  IP address returned (and cached)
  Browser ──9──► Web server 185.22.66.10 9  Page requested with HTTP/HTTPS
blocks.caption: Resolving www.nis.edu.kz

blocks.title: DNS lookup in words
items: The user types a **URL**; the browser first checks its own **cache** (and the computer's **hosts file**) for the IP address.
If it is not found, the computer sends the request to the **DNS resolver** of the ISP.
The resolver checks **its** cache; if not found, it asks a **root server**, which refers it to the **TLD server** (`.kz`).
The TLD server refers it to the **authoritative server** for the domain.
That server returns the **IP address**; the resolver **caches** it and sends it to the browser.
The browser connects to the **web server** using the IP address and requests the page.
If the name does not exist, an **error** is returned ("server not found").

blocks.content:
- **DNS spoofing / cache poisoning** — an attacker puts a **false IP address** into a DNS cache, sending users to a **fake website** (pharming).
- If DNS servers **fail** or are attacked (DDoS), websites cannot be reached by name even though they are working.
- Protection: **DNSSEC** (digitally signed records), HTTPS certificates, using trusted resolvers.

The full **address of a resource** (web page, file, image, video) on the Internet. It tells the browser **which protocol** to use, **which server** to contact and **where the resource is** on that server.

https://www.nis.edu.kz:443/en/students/timetable.html?class=11A#monday
└─┬─┘   └──────┬──────┘└┬┘└───────────┬───────────────┘└───┬───┘└──┬──┘
protocol    domain    port         path / file            query   fragment

rows: **How** to transfer the resource (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP)
**Which server**; converted to an IP address by **DNS**

blocks.title: More URLs
blocks.content:
- `http://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/George.jpg` — protocol **http**, host name **commons.wikimedia.org**, file location **/wiki/George.jpg**.
- `ftp://files.school.kz/homework/task1.pdf` — protocol **ftp** (file transfer).
- `https://www.google.com/search?q=binary+tree` — query **q=binary+tree**.

rows: A server, by an easy name
One **resource** on that server, with the protocol

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain how the domain name is used to access a website, including the role of DNS servers. [5]**
The user types the URL / domain name into the browser (1). The browser checks its **cache** for the IP address (1). If not found, a request is sent to the **DNS server (resolver)**, which holds / looks up a list of domain names and their **IP addresses** (1). If that server does not know it, the request is passed to **other DNS servers** up the hierarchy — root, TLD, authoritative (1). The **IP address is returned** to the browser (and cached), which uses it to **connect to the web server** and request the page (1).

**Q: Describe the relationship between the IP address and the domain name. [1]**
The IP address is the **numerical identifier** of the server that the domain name stands for (1).

**Q: Give one example of a URL indicating protocol, host name and file location. [1]**
`https://www.nis.edu.kz/en/timetable.html` (1).

**Q: State a second-level domain name of www.sk.nis.edu.kz. [1]**
**edu** (1).

- Saying DNS "stores websites" — it stores **names and IP addresses**, not pages.
- Reading domain levels from the **left** — read from the **right**.
- Confusing a **URL** (full address of a resource) with a **domain name** (one part of it).
- Forgetting the **cache** step in a DNS explanation.
